utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, if you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. All the accused are here, for the record. The witness is also present, already in the courtroom. Defence teams, it's a little bit confusing, as it is, but I notice the absence of Mr. Meek. That's all. The Prosecution, the same team as yesterday, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Mitchell. The four or five Defence experts are also present. I think we can safely start. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We left off yesterday with Exhibit 2884 up on the screen. This is the Susica operation map, with the artillery side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if you could maybe take yours out. I believe you just talked about it, and the Judge had asked the question, I believe, about what the little -- what the numbers meant that were next to the orange boxes which -- because we can see down in the key that the orange box is marked, in the English translation: "Fire with Howitzer 122 millimetre," but can give us any idea about those numbers. I'm talking just about the Srebrenica side of things now.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We don't have the corresponding document; that is, the target table for the orange boxes in the Srebrenica enclave. What it compares to, of course, is the target table that's listed on the right-hand part of this map corresponds to those boxes in Zepa. So, presumably, there's another document out there that we don't have or I've not seen that corresponds to these target numbers for the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's the significance of a target number?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can look at the document, and you'll see several columns, one of them is "Fire signal." A lot of artillery planning, of course, goes to preregistering fires and predesignating coordinates; and in the heat of battle, when everyone knows where the pre-planned fires can go, it's a lot easier on a commander to give a particular fire signal to have fire initiated in a certain area that's already been pre-registered, rather than it is to make a brand-new call for fire and have to pass trig coordinates over the radio, which can lend to mistakes. So this is part of the fire support and fire preparation plan that a headquarters staff would go through prior to the initiation of an operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's just talk briefly about what this map tells us about the Zepa targeting. You've got a target, a target table for Zepa, as you've just stated. We see various targets listed there, many of which are the -- identified as the enemy of the Muslim army. We also see the war hospital, and close to the village of Luke, and all the UN check-points, and the office of the military observers. Now, if an officer wanted to fire upon the office of military observers, what numbers on this target table would he use to do that, based on what you've just said?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you -- that's listed as target number 24, and the fire signal would be - and, again, forgive the pronunciation, "Siklon-74."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And what military reason would there be to fire on the military observers, the UN military observers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there was knowledge on the part of the VRS that perhaps that facility had been taken over by Bosnian Muslim forces, it would in fact, you know, be a legitimate target; but I can't figure out a reason why they would want to fire on the UN, absent that fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But to be clear, this was just a plan for something called "Susica" that we don't know anything about and didn't happen; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the planning process, we don't know anything that went off with this specific operation. However, as the other maps indicate, other operations - and last night in looking over one of the other maps, even the Krivaja 95 plan for the takedown of the Srebrenica enclave in July - these particular map graphics were used in that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- let's go on from there, and we're continuing, as your narrative continues, through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could ask the witness whether he has the actual knowledge as to the source of this map and when it was actually drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, the -- first, do you know where the OTP got this map from?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my understanding, sir, that these maps came from the documents known as the Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you -- I mean, as I think you've stated yesterday, we don't see a date anywhere on this map, but can you tell -- can you enlighten the Court and the rest of us on when you believe it may have, if at all possible - we, of course, don't want you to speculate - had been created?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indication of the operation Susica 95 certainly indicates 1995. From markings on other maps, and, in fact, by backing up to the initial exhibit, there are markings on this map that actually correspond to unit positions and axes of advance for the Krivaja 95. So while the original maps may have been created, I estimate, somewhere around April or May of 1995, there were penciled-in updates and markings on these all the way up to June and perhaps even early July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you think, don't you, that this is a spontaneous map drawn at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. These maps are part of a -- a prior planning process. There are, however, penciled-in updates to them. I believe the planning process occurred in the April/May 1995 time frame, pursuant to the broader directives under 7 and 7-1. But the penciled-in markings indicate that at least from a planning perspective, some individual in the Drina Corps, operations side, did use these maps and graphics and update them on a continual basis, as new variations of the plan may have been thought up or anything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Butler, let's continue in a chronological order, leading up to July 1995 in your narrative form.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 3028.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document from the Command of the Drina Corps, from its commander at the time, General Zivanovic. Now, May 27th, this is some ten days or so after the last set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to refresh your recollection, they called off that -- Mr. Butler has testified they called off that attack based on a document that said so due to personnel shortages and other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So now, ten days later, we see something entitled: "Based on the new situation at the front and around the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa and the apparent need to prevent the opening of the corridor between them and prevent enemy communications over our territory, and in order to prepare in time for bringing in forces and material in the area of engagement, I hereby ..." Then he issues orders to units that are listed here: The Milici Brigade, the Podrinje Brigade, others. What's this, Mr. Butler? How does this fit into your narrative?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I have this particular order in the narrative. It arrived later than the publication of my report. But what this document is is part of a deployment order associated with the VRS operation to take over the terrain around UN check-point Echo at Zeleni Jadar. What this order does is it directs the Commands of the 1st and 5th Podrinje units to send platoon-sized detachments to the Milici Brigade where they will be subsequently employed in supporting that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 3030.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is from the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade. I believe that is known as what brigade?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rogatica Brigade, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it's also dated 27 May, under the name of the commander of that brigade, Major Rajko Kusic. What's this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Major Kusic's order to his subordinates to form a company, and the details necessary: What ammunition they'll take, what transportation, who's responsible for executing the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't see, in either of these documents, any mention of Zeleni Jadar or any OP Echo or any UN check-point. How do you make the conclusion about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are additional documents, and I believe they will discuss them, that have to do with the Drina Corps order with respect to the detail of operations around Zeleni Jadar and the UN check-point Echo; as well as when one looks back at the Bratunac Brigade combat analysis of the six-month period, the Bratunac Brigade, of course, was part of that operation as well, and they listed as -- the operation's name is "Jadar-95."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 2669.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you've talked about before. This is the same date, May 27th, and it's an order from the Army of the Republika Srpska. This should be "Main Staff" - I think that's a mistranslation - to the command of various corpses. It's entitled "Order on induction and stationing of UNPROFOR members within the zone of responsibility of the corps," and it's in the name of Deputy Commander Lieutenant-General Manojlo Milovanovic. I won't go into detail, but it talks in paragraph 1 "for various commands to deploy captured prisoners of UNPROFOR and representatives of their international humanitarian organisations within their zones of responsibility." Now, what does this have to do with your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's just, in this context, you'll notice that there are a listing of corps; and on the second page, there is, under number 5, it reflects the fact that the Command of the Drina Corps shall placed captured UNPROFOR troops at installations in its area of responsibility. So while they did not get the first one, they did not get UN soldiers or other members as part of the first wave that was coming in from Sarajevo, given the context of upcoming military operations against the southern part of the enclave in Check-point Echo, if they were to capture or take custody of any UN soldiers, they were to be deployed to any location, such as warehouses or headquarters, in order to be used as a potential shield for NATO air strikes against those facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I don't want to get into the detail of all that, but were UN people taken prisoner?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was it in relation to air strikes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN's people who were captured in and around Sarajevo were captured, in part, in relation to the air strikes, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how were they used, just very briefly? I mean, for what reason were they used, not in particular how they were used?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was media coverage showing these individuals essentially being detained at military locations that NATO had shown a history of targeting or was considering targeting. They were being used, you know, as a way of pressuring NATO not to strike those facilities without killing their own soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did the -- did the VRS have success in this strategy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so did -- in your view, did it affect further air strikes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. My understanding is that air strikes were suspended shortly thereafter because of that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And will you, as we get towards Srebrenica, take this fact into consideration when looking at the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, not only was there, you know, an awareness as part of my analysis, but, I mean, as reflected in, you know, other documents and communications with the United Nations, as well as the VRS contact with the United Nations forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's -- let's keep moving forward beyond that period in late May and get to the period of early June, a document you've commented on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 2894.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's dated 2nd June, from the Command of the Drina Corps, in the name of General Zivanovic, and it's entitled: "Restoration of the control over the facilities on the Zeleni Jadar asphalt road." Can you fit this into your analysis that you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. From previous documents, as well as comments that General Zivanovic had made to UN members back in 1995, one of the comments that he made - probably shouldn't have made - was that he indicated to the UN that, "You'll know we're serious about taking over Srebrenica when we start coming back down and taking Zeleni Jadar." Tactically speaking, that's the main road that kind of came in from the southern part of the enclave down the hills towards Srebrenica, and the control of that Zeleni Jadar road area by the VRS was necessary to give them a proper staging area to begin an actual military operation against the town of Srebrenica in the future. So, yesterday, as I discussed, these are the time of preparatory military attacks that had to take place and missions that had to be accomplished before the stage could be set for the actual main assault on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And in this document, we can see, on the first page, a very specific spelling out, word for word, to soldiers on the ground of how to deal with the UNPROFOR people, just some of which says specifically: "I am warning you. Do not stand in my way." Then saying that they should fire a warning salvo; "Hands up, put down your weapons"; if they don't comply, fire a hand-held rocket, a Zolja; at the generator, to neutralise it; "Hands up; otherwise, I'm not responsible for your lives." Then, basically, after they surrender, "You're absolutely safe, my friends." Is this serious?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's serious in the context that the Drina Corps and, presumably, the Main Staff as well, there was not an intent there to not want to overtly attack the United Nations personnel and check-point in order to inflame the situation. What they wanted do, and you see this similar pattern in Srebrenica a month later, is they want to create the conditions through firing around the UN and pressuring the UN position, where they would voluntarily withdraw of their own accord. So they're not looking to -- in that sense, they're not looking to actually engage the UN directly and create a larger diplomatic and political problem than they already have at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So did this General Zivanovic's formula work in some -- in Srebrenica, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you take a look at the -- it's the second page in the English and B/C/S. It identifies a couple of people regarding after the UNPROFOR soldiers' surrender and, "They're absolutely safe, my friends." It says: "After that, Petrovic will call Nikolic, who will take UNPROFOR soldiers." Then it says: "Legenda and Petrovic shall take over the UNPROFOR check-point," and then,"further instructions." Can you tell us who you believe these the people are?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The individual listed as "Petrovic" is, in fact, Sreten Petrovic, the deputy commander of the 3rd Infantry Battalion of the Bratunac Brigade. "Nikolic" is Captain First Class Momir Nikolic, the chief of security for the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade. Milan -- Captain Milan Jolovic is the commander of the Drina Wolves organisation, which normally is subordinate to the Zvornik Brigade and to the Drina Corps. So those are the personalities involved in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 217.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us how this fits in?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is an order from the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade after their mission has been accomplished to take over the check-point, which reflects changes in the local unit dispositions, so they can now move the lines and defend the area more comprehensively that they have just taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to, actually, the next two exhibits, 65 ter 3011 and 3012.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: These are lists of Drina Corps duty officers and assistant duty officers for July 1995. Can you confirm, Mr. Butler, that that is what they are and that they were found as part of the Drina Corps collection?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The first document is the actual assignment of -- or the schedule of duty for the duty officers, and the second one is for the assistant or deputy duty officers for the month of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you just very briefly tell us the importance of the duty officer position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the -- given the fact that the commander and often the Chief of Staff is out visiting the units, the duty officer and the duty operations office is the focal point for incoming and outgoing communications of a particular unit. The, you know, phone calls that will come into various units will come in normally to the duty officer. He is, in effect, the commander's representative at the headquarters who is responsible for ensuring that the commander or the Chief of Staff or other staff sections are informed of developments as they come in from higher headquarters. He's also responsible for ensuring that reports and other forms of communication with the lower headquarters are done and brought to the higher headquarters as requested. So it's a fairly important position within the framework of any military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How many different duty officer positions are there in any -- in any particular, well, command or army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, generally, within the context of the VRS, what will you normally see, particularly at the brigade level, and in the corps level, is you'll have one duty officer and one or two duty assistants. In this context, it's -- it's not a designated duty. No one person is designated as a permanent duty officer. It's just part of a rotating schedule. Each officer in the command is expected to perform this duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned brigades, corps. Would the Main Staff have a duty officer as well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably, it would, sir, yes. I can't say that as a fact, but it should have a duty officer as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any records related to the Main Staff duty officer, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall if we do or not, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's continue on now, just getting into July 2nd, a 65 ter 2889.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a report from the Main Staff, dated 2 July, and the name of General Miletic, standing in as the Chief of Staff. I just want to refer you to the section on the Drina Corps, which is B/C/S page 3, English page 3. It talks a little about what's going on in the Drina Corps; and under section B, it says: "Unengaged forces are being prepared for the forthcoming active combat operations." Any idea what they're talking about there on July 2nd?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They're talking about the planning and movement of military forces related to the actual Krivaja 1995 operation. We know, from other sources of information with respect to the movement of officers from the Drina Corps, that they began their final reconnaissance and the initial part of their planning process as early as 30 June 1995. So this reflects an awareness at the Main Staff level that the Drina Corps and, presumably, you know, with the support of the Main Staff, is planning the Krivaja 95 operation as they're writing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next one, number 106, from the Command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's also dated 2 July, General Zivanovic. This is to the commands of several of the brigades, including the Zvornik Brigade and others. It gives some history about the Muslim offensive. Then it says, in paragraph 2: "The Command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to operation directive 7 and 7-1 of the Main Staff, and in view of the current situation at the front in its own area of responsibility, has to obtain forces for the intervention and repulsion of the enemy attacks to conduct active combat operations along the entire front, particularly towards Kladanj and Olovo." But we know directives -- the directives are pretty broad documents, and this talks about preparing operations on the entire front, mentioning Kladanj and Olovo. What, if anything, does this have to do with Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what they're doing, in this particular context, first you have to understand what a warning order is. A warning order is, in a military parlance, it is an order, not necessarily a preparatory order, but it is an order that is designed to give units that you are going to task with a particular mission the required preparatory time to start undertaking the things that they need to do, so that when you do give them the order, that they're prepared to do that. What they're doing in this particular context, while not saying "Srebrenica," is they are directing a number of brigades, the Zvornik Brigade, the Bihac Brigade, the Romanija Brigade, to assemble mobile forces. It tells them that they're going to be employed on an independent axes which is out of their particular area and the steps -- you know, and to start preparing those steps, knowing it's going to take one or two days to get these units assembled, again not revealing the ultimate objective. It says later on that at a point in time, "The plan will be coming to you." But the point of a warning order is to give the subordinate formation the maximum amount of time necessary to prepare what it needs to be able to do so that, in fact, when the order does come out, they've taken all the preparatory steps that they need to take so they can initiate the order. So you see this particular warning order to start mobilising formations for deployment out of the brigade areas, and you read it in concert with the actual attack order, and all of a sudden it makes sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did a subsequent -- did an order for Srebrenica come shortly thereafter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, if you could give me, tell me the difference between the warning order and preparatory order. I'm asking this because the 65 ter list of the Prosecution names this as a preparatory order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may be a victim of my own military terminology. This is what we would call a warning order. I don't know if somewhere the terms are being used interchangeably. A warning order, you know, it may very well be, like I say, the warning order, and it tells the unit to prepare for certain types of activities. So it may very well be the term is interchangeable. I don't think there's a difference in the term of art between a warning order and a preparatory order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because you said not necessarily a preparatory order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some degrees you will have a preparatory order which will be more much detailed, which will actually lay out the objectives and things of that nature. You don't necessarily have to have that degree of specificity in a warning order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't want to leave the impression that it's necessarily different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is dated 2 July, the same date as this warning order. This is a document entitled "Krivaja 95," from the Command of the Drina Corps, again from General Zivanovic. What's this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the actual combat order related to Krivaja 95 or the operation against the Srebrenica enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So that's not a whole lot of warning.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of a warning order is the recognition of the fact that the actual full plan is not fully fleshed out or completed yet; and, again, the goal of the warning order is to allow the subordinate units to take the steps that they need to take. In the beginning, they don't necessarily need to know the contents of the entire plan. So, you know, looking at a matter of timing, this may very well have come six, nine hours, even twelve hours after the initial warning order. Having said that, when you're trying to pull platoons or companies out of the front line and make sure that they're rested, that they're fully supplied, that their gear is done, you know, 12 hours can be very valuable to that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I'm not going to spend a lot of time with this, but I do want to ask you a couple of questions. The first page, we see some of the laying out of the Muslim forces and their activity. In fact, why don't you give us just a very brief historical update on the facts here, especially what the Muslim army has been doing in the -- in the spring, early summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly, what the Muslim forces have been doing is launching a series of offensives out of the 2nd Corps area, Tuzla, against Mount Majevica and the transmitter sites up on the mount. The 1st Corps out of Sarajevo has been launching offensive operations. And with respect to the activities of the 28th Infantry Division, what the 28th Infantry Division was specifically tasked to do was to conduct small-scale raids and military operations out of the enclave, with the goal of preventing the VRS and specifically the Drina Corps from pulling forces away from those enclaves and sending them to more important areas of the front lines. So their job was, essentially, to take whatever military actions they could in order to tie down the VRS away from where the main attacks were going in the 1st and 2nd Corps area; and, in fact, they engaged in those types of raids against Serb military and village positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, just briefly, do you know where the most significant supplies -- military supplies came from for the 28th Division to be able to conduct these sorts of operations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, the land route was what's commonly known as the smuggling trail that originates in Muslim territory actually near the Zvornik Brigade area, near Tuzla; and it transits through the Zvornik Brigade zone and the Bratunac Brigade zone through the valleys, and allowed them to bring equipment and supplies, small arms, things of that nature, over-land. I believe that there has also been ample evidence that the Bosnian Muslim military did, in fact, commission clandestine helicopter flights from Tuzla into the enclave in order to drop off war materials such as ammunition, money or pay for the soldiers, evacuate wounded, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And does this plan lay out several military targets in and around the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. It's a fairly comprehensive plan. It lays out -- as a first component, it lays out the VRS's understanding of the military situation on the ground with respect to the deployments of the 28th Infantry Division; and, again, going back to the map graphics that we discussed earlier for Susica, this is -- you know, these are almost identical. So, in this context, you know, the VRS is fairly certain in its mind -- you know, it understands what the enemy environment looks like inside the -- the enclave. The second component, again referencing operation directive 7 and 7-1 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that is on B/C/S page 2, English page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- starts talking about, particularly in paragraph 4, what the corps commander has directed to take place, in broader terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me get you specifically back, though, to paragraph 2, where as you say, it states: "The Command of the Drina Corps, pursuant to operations directive 7 and 7-1 of the Main Staff, and on the basis of the situation in the corps area of responsibility, has the task of carrying out offensive activities with free forces deep in the Drina Corps zone as soon as possible in order to split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica and to reduce them to their urban areas." First of all, you've already cited to directive 7 and 7-1, so let me just ask you: What, in your view, does it mean to "split apart the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: While they are physically separated, obviously, on the ground and in a map, those supplies that were brought in to Srebrenica, those military supplies, it was the expectation that the 28th Division would also send a portion of those supplies down to, you know, the Zepa Brigade, which was considered to be a component part of the 28th. When they talk about splitting the enclaves apart, what they are referring to is essentially completing the defence lines of the blockade, so that the Muslim military forces inside the Srebrenica enclave can no longer over-land supply the Muslim forces in Zepa, or the Muslim forces in Zepa cannot travel over-land into Srebrenica. There was a fairly active land route that those military forces were using, and one of the themes from 1993 on was the, you know, attempts by the VRS to cut those land communications between Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You use the word that there was -- the VRS had an "expectation" that this would be used, and then you went on to what you just said. Was this more than just an expectation on the part of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, the VRS knew that the supplies were going from Srebrenica to Zepa and had tried, unsuccessfully for years, to be able to block the supply line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next part of this, after splitting the enclaves, was "to reduce them to their urban areas." You've talked briefly about this before, but now we see it in this plan. Can you just say what you think they mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, as I indicated earlier, you know, the way that I read this, based on the situation in May 1993 and subsequent information in documents or even interviews and statements, is that the VRS never recognised the broader designated safe area that was around Srebrenica that we call the enclave. Their view was the only part that they ever agreed to was that area immediately surrounding the urban area or the actual town of Srebrenica. So this goes back to, you know, a one-kilometre by two-kilometre area centred on the, you know, downtown Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what, in your view, was -- would be the situation if the enclaves were, in fact -- or the Srebrenica enclave was, in fact -- sorry, both enclaves were reduced to their urban area?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, you stopped Mr. McCloskey asking that question two days ago. He's asked it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Haynes is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we go down into paragraph 4, as you've stated, we got to the objective to separate in size the Srebrenica enclave and "to improve the tactical position of the forces in the depth of the area and to create conditions for the elimination of the enclaves." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in several keys, by improving the tactical positions and in the depth of the area, by bringing the VRS front lines closer to the town of Srebrenica, on more favourable terrain, as well as bringing it closer to the town of Zepa, it gives the VRS units a lot more depth in their rear areas, which means if the Muslims are going to smuggle material, they have far, far greater distance to go through enemy territory to do it, which would make it that much harder. "At the same time creating the conditions for the elimination of the enclaves," I read that to, again, be the same type of situation that they had created in May of 1993, where they want to create an environment; whereas, the -- either on their own accord, the Muslims would leave the enclave or that the UN would evacuate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you mean -- when you say "1993", what do you mean, in particular? What event or time period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the situation in May of 1993, when, as a result of the earlier VRS military operations, the VRS forces were surrounding the town of Srebrenica, and you had the Muslim military forces as well as this large civilian population of Muslims all crowded in the town. And at that point in time, you actually had the undertaking of evacuations. I believe some eight to ten thousand civilians were pulled out of the town by the UN as part of evacuations until they were stopped. So they're trying to recreate that situation in order to create the conditions that that decision will again start and the UN will evacuate the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is dated the next day. It's a report from the Main Staff in the name of General Miletic, still standing in for the Chief of Staff. Just going briefly to the Drina Corps section, it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, thank you. 65 ter 2890.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on page 3 of the B/C/S, page 3 of the English, there's a -- there's a short line that says: "Forces that are not engaged are carrying out preparations for forthcoming active combat operations." And, briefly, Mr. Butler, what does that tell us, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects the awareness of the Main Staff of what's going on in the zone of the Drina Corps and that they're keeping their superior commands informed. In this case, it would be the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 3025.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you do so, since you didn't seem to recollect what Mr. Haynes pointed out and what we agreed with, we refer you to yesterday's transcript, page 19707, lines 1 to 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You know, I have no -- no doubt, especially when you agree with Mr. Haynes, so I thank you very much. All right. Let's -- we're at 65 ter 3025.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's dated 5 July 1995, the next day. This is a document in the name of Commander Colonel Blagojevic of the Bratunac Brigade, and it makes reference, in the right-hand corner, of Krivaja 95 and order for active combat operations, and it appears to be partly a repeat of the Drina Corps order. Mr. Butler, can you tell us, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, it was fairly customary in their orders process that, in large respects, the subordinate formation would mimic the language of the orders and directives from the superior formation, in part to make sure that everyone understood they were on the same framework for what the commander had intended. It's changed insomuch as it gives more specific orders that are directed towards their subordinate formations. So it's just additional detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 4 in the English, B/C/S page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Under "Tasks," 6.1.1, it talks about: "Open fire on observed targets in the sectors of Potocari school, Pasica, Budak, Pale, and Cizmici." It says: "Prevent the enemy from introducing fresh forces from their depths towards to their positions." But what I want to ask you about is it says: "Open barrage fire in the Potocari sector in case of possible attack and prevent withdrawal of UN weapons towards the depth of the enclave." Why would they want to prevent withdrawal of the UN weapons towards the depth of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tactically speaking, where most of the UN's combat power was with respect to armoured vehicles was that they were out at the deployed check-points along the perimeter, in some cases along the perimeter where there was no attack planned. One of the intents that they wanted to be able to do was, at least in their mind by putting this together, to prevent the United Nations, the Dutch Battalion forces, from pulling all of their armoured vehicles and other combat power away from spread-out locations and to concentrate that combat power, which would make it far more difficult and allow the Dutch a much more increased ability to defend the enclave if they elected to do so. It was much more tactically desirable to have the Dutch forces scattered out all over the width of the enclave, rather than have them concentrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know, is there any indication that the VRS ever had to do that, ever had to actually physically prevent UNPROFOR to do this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't believe there were any instances where the VRS targeted the UN deployed check-points with the goal of preventing them from withdrawn from their positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there targeting, though, and I don't want to get into a lot of that, but was there targeting, in your view, by the VRS on the UN check-points or other UN targets?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. They did target the UN, again with the goal of having them abandon those positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I -- this is a -- makes reference to some artillery targets, and I just -- I won't take us back to the document. But back to General Zivanovic's plan, it says, on page 5 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S, that: "During a preparatory fire to neutral the enemy targets as a plan for preparatory fire." Did you ever, or did the OTP ever, in your possession have -- in your knowledge, have possession of an artillery plan such as we've seen from those maps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bratunac Brigade, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For anything to do with the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I don't think we've ever had the actual targeting plan, the written document that goes with it, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And under 6.2, there's a notation: "At 0300 hours on 6 July 1995, it will fire four projectiles (50 kg air bombs)," which if we look at the original, it talks about Avijo Bombi, "on the Potocari sector, the school, the 11th March Factory in the Gracic hills," and then it is "Kula and Orici." What's a 50 kg avio-bomb or air bomb?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ordinance as designed was just what it says, it's in fact a bomb designed to be dropped by an aircraft against a ground target. In the latter part of the war, what the VRS armaments industry started engaging in the practice of was trying to modify these weapons or this ordinance to be used in a ground type of environment by ground forces. You saw it a lot in Sarajevo and in Western Bosnia. It dealt with the issue of, you know, homemade -- homemade modifications by the RS Defence Ministry or the defence industry to potentially weld or put rockets on the back of these weapons, so you could push or propel them off of rail launchers in the general direction of the enemy that you were targeting. They were not particularly accurate weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And these target lists that they give, do you have any reason to believe any of those are either civilian or UN targets?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do. I believe the facility known as the 11th March Factory was, in fact, one of the buildings that the UN was using.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's -- let me go back -- well, excuse me. No, let's continue there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On page 5 of the English and the B/C/S, Colonel Blagojevic notes that: "Prisoners of war and war booty will be collected in Pribicevac sector." He underlines "Comply with the Geneva Convention," and then he underlines again "in the treatment of prisoners of war and the population." So is that a reference that certainly Colonel Blagojevic was aware of the conventions and the regs that you'd talked about previously?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, I certainly can't attest that he might have personally underlined it; but the fact that it is in this order, it is signed by him, Colonel Blagojevic is aware of these provisions; and, again, also the fact that Pribicevac is the location not only of the forward command post of the Drina Corps but also of the Bratunac Brigade. So he wants to make sure these people are assembled in the position where presumably down the line they can quickly be questioned for any information of tactical value.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go to -- I just want to skip ahead in time to a document the Court has seen. It makes a reference -- in English, it's called "aerosol bomb." And if we look at the B/C/S, it's something very similar to that, "arisolnir" or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That is at 65 ter 2517.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't want to get into the details of this. This is a 21 July document by General Tolimir relating to Zepa and the Muslims, and Muslim refugees, and the Muslim army. And in paragraph 5, it says: "The most convenient means of their destruction would be usage of chemical weapons or aerosol grenades and bombs."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I should be more clear. I think he's referring to the army in that context. I didn't mean to suggest he was referring to the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is this aerosol bomb anything related to this avio or air bomb that you talked about, in your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. They are different weapons systems. The aerial -- the aerosol grenade or bomb is what we would call in the West a fuel-air explosive. It's a weapon that takes advantage of the physics behind vapours being more explosive than solids; and for the weight and size, you get a much greater blast and shock effect from the weapon than you would with conventional munitions. It's particularly effective against structures that you want to knock down, and it's very effective as an antipersonnel role. The blast overpressurisation has a particularly lethal effect on soldiers at a far greater range than conventional explosives do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How does it work, just briefly? How is it delivered?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be delivered either by an aircraft-delivered device or by a large rocket. What it is is it's a system that, as it gets close to its target, it's parachute-retarded, so it slows down. It starts ejecting explosive vapour out; and at a certain concentration where that vapour becomes explosive, an igniter of some device will go off, creating a spark which will, of course, ignite that vapour. Basically, it's the same principle of why you don't smoke while filling up your gas tank at the fuel station. It's not the gasoline that gets you, it's the gasoline vapours that can cause an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your view, is there anything illegal about that weapon?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document. We're going ahead in time, 6 July 1995. This is 65 ter 233.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a daily combat report from 6th July, the date that we were talking about in the previous document by Colonel Blagojevic. Just to refer you down to paragraph 2, it says: "Firing support against set targets was provided by 50 kg," and now we have a new word in English, "shell launcher," and then it has those same sites, school in Potocari, 11 March Factory. Can you make out what that means, that part about 50 kg shell launcher?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I believe we're talking about the same weapons system that's described as the, you know, aerial bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not the aerosol bomb?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Staying now with July 6th, the Main Staff report to the Presidency, 65 ter 2895; and, again, in the name of General Miletic standing in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the zone of the Drina Corps, and referring you to the part that says: "The forces have been prepared and grouped for active combat operations towards the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, a technical question. Could we have the corresponding page in B/C/S, because the accused are -- cannot follow if they don't have the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 3. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame Fauveau. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. They have it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Okay. I'm being informed that the text is in front of the accused. They can see it. They can follow from there. Correct me if I am wrong, but this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, they have the first page only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I left out the "page 3."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's there, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time, it's okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Page 3, B/C/S, 4 in English. That also reminds me. Ms. Fauveau, just to clear up an issue with Ms. Fauveau yesterday, when she mentioned the document that she read that did not have the term - it was number 414 - did not have the term "operations officers" in it, our team interpreter has reviewed that and agrees with Ms. Fauveau. It's the term "referent," which gets interpreted in many different ways, but we think "administrators" or "administrative officers" is a fair translation, and we actually have a revised translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Again, this section on B/C/S page 3: "The forces have been prepared and grouped for active combat operations towards the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa. Upon receiving an interim report, we will inform you of the combat results." Is this correct, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The actual ground operation began the morning of 6th July. Given that the regular combat report for the Drina Corps is normally drafted at the main headquarters in Vlasenica, everyone would be dependent upon an interim report by, at that time, it would be General Krstic, the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps at the IKM, for details pertaining to how the actual attack at Srebrenica was being conducted and how it was going according to plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's now go to 8 July, to the next document, 65 ter 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a one-page document from the Drina Corps Command to the forward command post, General Krstic personally, and to Major-General Zdravko Tolimir for information at the Main Staff, from General Zivanovic. What do you make of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- you know, when you look at the context of this, this appears to be the VRS's response to a complaint raised by UNPROFOR that their forces are being attacked by the VRS. Knowing how that system worked during the period, it looks like, you know, the complaint was made to General Tolimir, some other official at the Main Staff. There's been a discussion with General Zivanovic. General Zivanovic is now talking to his subordinate at the time, which would be General Krstic, as well as keeping General Tolimir informed about what he's telling his subordinate commander. So that's what the context of this particular order depicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I note it says: "The Main Staff has ordered you not to attack UNPROFOR, but to prevent any surprises and stop the Muslims in their intention to join up Srebrenica." What do you make of that, given that there's a complaint to -- that they've been attacked?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I've discussed prior and in my narrative, of course, the basic method that they wanted to use to get around or through the UN check-points was not to directly attack them. It was to fire over their heads, fire on the side, keep edging up, you know, the goal being to achieve the desired result of gaining the territory without the political risk of actually firing at United Nations soldiers. So this is a reiteration of that. You're not supposed to be attacking the UNPROFOR directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I won't ask you about whether UNPROFOR knows they're being attacked or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 9 July 1995, Exhibit 6D00022.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document, an interim combat report from General Krstic, at that time the Chief of Staff, and it talks about the, as we see, the developing combat situation and the success. How does this document fit into your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you go back to the original 2 July order for Krivaja 95, and you look at the specific tasks of each of the units, what this combat report is essentially reporting is that they have reached all of their primary objectives, and now the stages are set for further operations. So, in some respects, it's letting them know that, "We've achieved the lines that we've wanted to do." You know, "What's the next step in the plan here?" The other part of it is, reporting up the chain, that they have taken a number of UN soldiers and equipment into custody, and further explains where they are being accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe some of them were accommodated in Milici and others were taken to Bratunac. They eventually ended up at the Hotel Fontana.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 3018.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And before I get there, everyone knows that the Hotel Fontana is not very far from the base in Potocari. Have you made any conclusion regarding why the VRS kept those soldiers in the Hotel Fontana as opposed to just getting them back to the -- Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably, they -- they could have potentially taken them through the yellow bridge check-point, but, you know, their intent was probably just to hold on to these soldiers at the Hotel Fontana and other locations. I don't -- I don't know why they wouldn't have returned them back to UN custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On 11 July, is -- does anything occur relating to those -- those UN members in the custody of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, again, whether it's by specific design or by default, those members of the UN who are in custody of the VRS are, in fact, used as leverage, and threats are made or implied against them in order to force the NATO forces to suspend bombing VRS units and positions around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that have any success, those threats against the UN hostages in the Srebrenica context, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did; and, in fact, as a result of that, the bombing was suspended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back in time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I need to leave the courtroom for one minute or two minutes. In the meantime, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's on 9 July, 65 ter 3018, which I see is up there, from Tolimir to General Krstic personally, and General Tolimir personally for information. First of all, is General Tolimir sending something to himself? Does that make -- I mean, it may not be a big issue, but do you know why that would be? Perhaps we have a translation issue. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, it means being sent from the Drina Corps, and, you know, the fact is when you look at the context of the conversation, the message that's being left is for General Tolimir. So, I mean, the fact that they want to make sure General Tolimir is informed about what's happening is normal protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But this appears to be authored by General Tolimir, is my point.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, he's located at the Drina Corps Command while he's sending it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the top left-hand side, the "Drina Corps Command and Intelligence Security Department, 7/184," that's one of their sequence numbers, that's not a Main Staff sequence number. It may very well just be he wanted to have a paper copy of what this message said, to make sure he had it available at the Main Staff when he got back there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what do you make of the substance of this communication?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it basically discusses in substance a conversation with General Nikolai, reflecting the fact that, you know, they're concerned about the incursion into the enclave. What General Tolimir is doing is essentially temperising, basically saying, "We don't have --" you know, "We think we're fighting the BiH. We don't have the same information you do. I will check the information you have," and making sure that -- you know, telling the forces they're safe and noting that he is going to talk to them in 40 minutes. What he obviously wants is he's letting -- you know, he's letting the military commanders know on the ground that he's getting pressured by the UN, and he's letting them know what he's telling the UN. The final context of that is a request that says, you know, "Please check in," you know, "as often as possible." Every hour, he would like a report, so he can give the best, not necessarily the most accurate, information to the UN, so that he has the most accurate information in order to say whatever plausible story he wants the UN to hear in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does this document indicate in any way that, in your view, that General Tolimir is not aware of what's really going on on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, I believe he fully is. When he's at the Drina Corps, where he would have been briefed, in his last line: "I congratulate you on your results, and I wish you the good fortunes of war." I mean, clearly General Tolimir knows exactly what the plan is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 236, 9 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a combat report from the Bratunac Brigade, and I just want to refer you to what's on the first page of the B/C/S and page 4 in English, the last line. It says: "Two UNHCR vehicles with 15 UNPROFOR soldiers who fled to our territory were brought into the brigade command and have been put up in the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac." Is that related to what you've said earlier?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, somewhere during the course of the operation, the UN check-points were given the authority by their commander to -- depending on what they felt was the safest course of action was, they could withdraw through the combat area or through the Muslim lines or they could put themselves in the custody of the VRS. I believe, in this particular context, most of the UN check-points elected to put themselves into the custody of the VRS rather than try and transit through Muslim lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, in one case, did that prove very dangerous for the UN, to go through Muslim lines?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The only Dutch soldier killed was, in fact, killed by a grenade thrown by a Muslim soldier at the UN forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 849.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a one-page document, and this time it says: "From the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska," from General Tolimir: "Very urgent," to the president of Republika Srpska for information, Drina Corps, forward command post, Generals Gvero and Krstic personally. First of all, can you -- do you have any idea where Tolimir is during this communication?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: During this particular communication, based on where the order originated, I believe he's at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we -- we've all read this many times. Can you just give us your brief take on this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular document is the first document that I've seen of the broader collection of material in the possession of the OTP that reflects that because of the success of the combat operations, now, for the first time, the goal is going to be expanded and it will actually be the occupation of the very town of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what can you tell from the fact that this is directed to Generals Gvero and Krstic personally?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Krstic is the man at the forward command post of the Drina Corps in Pribicevac, controlling the operation and directing it. General Gvero, the Main Staff officer, is present at that location as well. This is sent to them primarily for the benefit of General Krstic, to tell him that, you can, "You need to start putting together the next step." There are no plans to take Srebrenica, so it's giving him the directive to start doing the steps you need to take, planning wise and force-movement wise, to occupy the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Does General Gvero's presence at the forward command post have any significance for you in your overall analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, other than it's just a -- again a reflection of the practice where, in critical operations, that often officers of the Main Staff will be present at these command posts to help oversee the operations and be there as a person who can potentially de-conflict any problems between the corps and the Main Staff with respect to resources, with respect to orders, with respect to understanding what the overall Commander Mladic's intent is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And, again, we see in this document a full understanding of the Geneva Conventions, and there's an actual order not to torch residential buildings and to treat the population and war prisoners in accordance with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General Tolimir, this is the person that talks about aerosol bombs and refugees. How do you -- can -- does General Tolimir appear to be the author of this document or would this be a document passed on? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the bottom of the document -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I'll object. I think it mischaracterises the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can move on. You're not necessarily right, but we can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can explain, if the Court wishes, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just need to reference the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just move on, please, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next document in line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're now at 10 July, a document you've already talked about. It's 65 ter 57, but that was for your legal discussion. And what I wanted to ask you about is: Do you know, from your review, where Mr. Borovcanin was prior to 11 July, when he had to go to the Bratunac/Srebrenica area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand that Mr. Borovcanin was directing MUP forces along the Trnovo battle front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And do you have any knowledge about whether or not he was working with any forces from Serbia in that Bosnian battle front at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it's related within paragraph 2 of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you're referring to a mixed company of joint RSK -- sorry, not "RSK" but Serbian and RS forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Has the investigation ever corroborated or identified any Serbian MUP forces involved in the Srebrenica/Bratunac operations of 11 July through 17/18 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It might be a good time, Mr. President, to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're still on July 10th in our chronology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 181.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document from the Main Staff, dated 10 July, in the name of General Mladic, and we see a received stamp of about 1300 hours. And on the first page of the B/C/S, this order talks about the newly-arisen situation at Srebrenica and the success, and provides an order apparently in the direction of Zepa. What do you make of this, on 10 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, when I discussed earlier about, you know, thinking tactically about the battle on the ground and then thinking operationally about what happens beyond that, this is a good example of the Main Staff thinking operationally, presumably at the direction of General Mladic. They're already beginning to take the next series of steps with respect to planning and manoeuvring forces based on what they call the unexpected success of Srebrenica, and they're already thinking through about the potential for engaging in combat activity in Zepa along the same way. So this is a reflection that, you know, the Main Staff isn't, you know, totally engrossed in the current battle,. They're already thinking through the mechanics of what needs to happen to set the framework for the next battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this appears to only go to the Drina Corps and the 65th Protection Regiment. What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps and the 65th, you know, the Drina Corps, Zepa is in their zone, and the 65th Protection Regiment are local forces who are at -- garrisoned in and around the Main Staff, which is, of course, close to Zepa, that, you know, could be used in this operation. At this juncture, they're not envisioning having any outside forces from the Drina Corps participate. They're going to try and deal with this on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There's no -- this is not sent to any brigades at this point, why not, if you can -- if you know or have an opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I mean, this is, you know, not necessarily something that is particularly urgent, where you would see the Main Staff send it to the Drina Corps and the brigades. This is something that can go along the more formalised line. It goes through the corps' command and staff, telling them, "Start and," you know, "plan to launch offensive operations. Here's where you will set unit boundaries." The expectation is that the operations people at the Drina Corps will start delving into the details of this, and they will send out the detailed orders to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And a little later on, do we see an order from the Drina Corps, a more operational order about Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's within the next day or two. It may be as early as the 11th or the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll -- we'll get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to now 11 July, Exhibit 6D00207.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're going to 19, Mr. Butler, on your tab, and this is an 11 July document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've put the old translation in here because it was, I believe, already in evidence, but it's General Staff of the Army - and that should be "Main Staff," we'd all agree - 11 July, in the name of Assistant Commander Major General Milan Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's received it seems by somebody it looks like at about 1735 hours, entitled: "Warning on treatment of UNPROFOR personnel in the enclave of Srebrenica." It says: "In relation to the total situation in the enclave of Srebrenica, the monitoring of reactions from UNPROFOR representatives and world public opinion indicates that the attitude of the Army of Republika Srpska personnel towards UNPROFOR personnel and units in the area of Srebrenica is in the focus of attention. "To that end, Drina Corps command, acting through its subordinate commands, will ensure utmost decency in the attitude towards UNPROFOR personnel, our guests, and prevent any actions or provocations directed against UNPROFOR units in the enclave, regardless of their behaviour. "Such attitude towards UNPROFOR units is at this moment of multifarious importance for the realisation of the assignment at hand and of our set objectives." What's your analysis of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this juncture, General Gvero, who was at the IKM, is apparently back at the Main Staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we know that, for example, we have documents which show him at the IKM on the 9th. We know, from other documents and other information, that General Mladic shows up at the IKM personally on the 10th. With General Mladic on the scene, there's no reason for General Gvero to be there as the Main Staff representative. General Mladic can obviously do that better than anyone else. So General Gvero goes back to his position or back to his headquarters at the Main Staff. And, you know, in this context, it's clear that once he's arriving back there, he's taking the pulse of what the media, what the International Community, is saying about the operations related to Srebrenica and the fact that UN personnel are in VRS custody, and reminding them that, you know, "People from the outside, the International Community, are looking at us. Let's make sure we put our best face on."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you take about this comment, "Such attitudes towards UNPROFOR units is at this moment are of multiple importance"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly, when you look in light of what happened in May, when VRS were taking UN personnel as hostage, considering that at this time there were public pronouncements with respect to potential NATO involvement in protecting the Dutch Battalion at Srebrenica and that these conversations are happening in the media and diplomats and politicians are making these related comments, General Gvero is trying to remind people, you know, "Let's not give the International Community or NATO any pretext whatsoever to become involved in this fight."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at this time, this would be around the late afternoon or evening, have there been any actions directed against UN -- I don't mean "actions." Had the UN people that had held hostage, the UNPROFOR people - excuse me - held in the Hotel Fontana, have there been any statements by the VRS about them regarding their treatment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is a fair example of a good military idea that was overcome by events. For example, while General Gvero was potentially drafting this, in the meantime NATO forces had already begun to strike VRS targets on at least two occasions at the edge of the enclave. And before this message is even delivered to the IKM, which is where I believe it went, a threat had been communicated to Dutch-Bat that if UN or NATO air forces did not stop bombing, that there would be retaliation against Dutch soldiers in the custody of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, such a threat, at what level of the Army of the VRS or the political apparatus would such a threat be, in your view, allowable under the organisation of this government and army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that anyone below General Mladic, personally, would feel that they had the authority to make such a -- such a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And would such a threat --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we can go on. Let's continue to go on, on 11 July, 65 ter 438, from the Drina Corps Command by General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's the concern in this document, briefly, entitled: "Order to block the linking up of the forces of the 28th Enemy Division with forces in the enclaves"? We see a received stamp about 2230 hours on the 11th.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the VRS, just like the BiH, was doing what it could to collect information about what Muslim military forces -- their goals and objectives were. The information that they were receiving at the time indicated that the 28th Division was going to be given instructions to leave the enclave, which left one of two possible scenarios: One, that they would attempt to link up, either in whole or in part, with the Muslim forces that were still in the enclave in section; or that, two, that they would attempt to break out of the enclave and get to what's referred to as "free territory," Bosnian Muslim territory, opposite Tuzla. So, in keeping in line with what this order is, it's General Zivanovic directing units of the Drina Corps to be aware of those facts and to take precautionary measures to prevent this from happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell from this document if the VRS has had any knowledge about which direction they're actually going in at this point on the 11th; the Muslim forces, that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, they're making an estimate. They don't know exactly which course of action the Muslims will take.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
