utterances.text: Staying at 11 July, but going to 65 ter 3019, this is another report from the Main Staff under the name of General Miletic, to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go to B/C/S page 3, I just want you to check the information in this. It talks about: "In the Srebrenica enclave, the enemy has been putting up fierce resistance to VRS units. The NATO air force has been pounding our forces in the following sectors." It talks about an interim report will be sent. It goes on to talk about: "In the course of the day, our forces entered the town of Srebrenica, and we will forward you an interim report on the results achieved and the details relating to the offensive operations." Do you agree with this or disagree with this information, as to its validity?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think -- I'm quite sure at this juncture the Court has seen the video footage of VRS forces and officers entering the town of Srebrenica, and this corresponds to that, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's now go to the 12th, and we have a 65 ter 1099A for English, and B/C/S, 1099C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a very brief intercept between X and Y, talking about Jaglici, from Jaglici towards Buzim: "Up there towards the neighbour on our right, let them know they need to be warned. You understand." "Understood, a column." What do you think this is at 063 -- 0603 hours in the morning?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I determined to be the first plausible piece of information that begins going up through the VRS information chain of command, that they are noticing that the VRS, at least the people on the ground, are noticing the establishment of a column and that there are Bosnian Muslim in the forces at that location, and that they're trying to penetrate the VRS lines at that particular location. Taken in context with the understanding the VRS had at the time, their view was that the most -- most of the 28th Division was, in fact, going to retreat towards the Bandera Triangle and potentially go to Zepa, and, in fact, the VRS operations scheduled for 12 July 1995 had the bulk of their combat power sweeping through that particular area in order to attempt to regain contact and engage the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when you say "that particular area," which one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bandera Triangle area, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, at least now you're getting indications from VRS soldiers in other parts of the battlefield that the division isn't where everyone had expected it to be. It is, in fact, doing something completely unexpected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so Jaglici, that's up in the direction towards Konjevic Polje, on towards Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next intercept, number 1100A, and in English, and C in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's, again, dated 12 July, 0656 hours, and there's comments in here related to similar areas: "They inform me first at 3.00 that it was broken in several parts."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please read slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, again, we hear "Jaglici, Kamenica." What's this, just briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is another intercept between two correspondents, discussing their knowledge of the military actions, where the column is, what they're attempting to do, at roughly 7.00 in the morning on 12 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this consistent with previous intercept, that the column is going in the direction?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, again, there's no hard facts on how large the column is, how powerfully armed it is. You're getting that these represent the initial battlefield reports and contact that's coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So this kind of information at this -- at this stage, as initial reports, how do you, as an intel analyst, would you have valued that at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a -- there's a saying, particularly in my military with respect to combat information, that the first report is wrong, the second report is only half right, you don't know which part of the report is, in fact, correct. It isn't until the third or fourth report that you start to get a clear picture of what is actually happening in a particular battle or a particular situation. I think what you're seeing, you know, in broad terms, is a manifestation of that. As these events are occurring on the ground and more and more reports about them are being passed up the chain of command, it's going to take a while, but people are now starting to get a little bit of a clearer picture that their initial assessments on where the 28th Infantry Division were might not be completely accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit, 1101A and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another intercept. It's 12 July at 0735 hours in the morning, between people identified as Krstic and Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic. Who are these guys, and briefly what are they talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this conversation, the individual named "Krstic" is Major-General Radislav Krstic, still the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. Lieutenant-General Krsmanovic is the transportation officer for the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what are they talking about, in your view?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, just bear in mind that what the Judges are following it a bit slower than appears. It now appears. Now we have the intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I will keep my eye on that screen, and I think we're on track to finishing this week, so I should slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I fully understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll slow myself down a bit. Thank you. Okay. We all have this now, this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what are these people talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we have is General Krstic is informing his transportation officer where he wants buses sent and at what location and at what time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what relevancy are buses at this point to the Drina Corps, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at the broader knowledge of what happened with the series of the two meetings that occurred between the VRS, the UN Dutch forces, and the representatives of the Bosnian Muslims on the 11 -- on the evening 11 July at Fontana, some time after that series of meetings, either at the back end or shortly thereafter, the VRS, General Mladic specifically, you know, took it upon himself that, you know, the VRS was going to organise the evacuation of these individuals from Potocari. They didn't want to wait for the UN. They didn't want to give the opportunity for the UN and the UNPROFOR to stall. He wanted these people out. He wanted them out in a quick manner. And very quickly after that, through the evening of the 11th and the morning of the 12th, there's a lot of messages and orders going out for buses that are under control of the army and buses that are under control of the Ministry of Defence or state-owned industries to start being sent to Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, this says: "Fifty buses in total are to be at the stadium in Bratunac by 1700 hours." Did they make it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the first evidence of buses started arriving as early as noon on the 12th of July in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure when buses may have arrived at the Bratunac stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 110.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is dated 12 July, from the Command of the Drina Corps, in the name of General Zivanovic, and we see now that it is entitled: "The provision of buses for evacuation from the Srebrenica enclave," order to the Zvornik Brigade and other brigades. What is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It amplifies what I've been talking about with respect to the last series of exhibits, the fact that formal orders have been going out through the early-morning hours of 12 July to military and Ministry of Defence organisations for them to take the measures to organise their buses and start sending them to the Srebrenica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when you say "their buses," the Zvornik Brigade, for example, what buses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Each of the brigades had some buses or some form of transportation. The Zvornik Brigade was better than most, and they had some minibuses and some trucks. Up in Zvornik, also you had the 63rd Auto Transport Battalion which had vehicles. But the majority of buses were going to have to be requisitioned from the civilian economy, and that falls more in the purview of the RS Ministry of Defence than it does strictly the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 1105A and B, and an intercept from 12 July, at 9.15 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is just a synopsis of a conversation, and it says, with Lieutenant-Colonel Krsmanovic: "They told him that they only have two buses. They can't requisition without papers and an order. They have problems with fuel. There is none." You've talked a bit about requisitioning. How does this fit, if it does?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it does in the sense that, you know, they understand what the process is, and it's a reflection of the fact that, you know, even General Mladic can't snap his finger and demand, you know, 50 to 100 buses to show up instantly and it's going to happen. There is a lot of planning, there is a lot of logistics, there's a lot of coordination that has to happen to carry out that order. Normally, you plan for these things so you're not in a situation like the VRS finds itself in the circumstance, where they're trying to organise these large-scale bus convoys on the fly. So what you see in the intercepts, you know, are the reflections of these various staff officers who are trying to do, as fast as they can, take all the necessary steps to acquire the buses, make sure they have adequate fuel, make sure they have drivers, make sure they know where they're supposed to be, and when they're supposed to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. This comment about "they have problems with fuel," can you briefly describe the fuel situation for the VRS and RS at this time in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because of the embargo which prevented fuel from flowing freely over the Drina River and the Serbian border, fuel was a valuable commodity to not only the VRS but well within the Republika Srpska at the time. It was a very popular black market item, as you might imagine. Therefore, to ensure that the military supply of fuel was properly guarded and properly regulated, the VRS took great steps to make sure that their fuel was accounted for on a litre-by-litre basis, so they weren't wasted fuel and they could ensure fuel was not being siphoned off by members of the military for private purposes. At the same time, you know, those same procedures were in place, you know, throughout the state-owned economy and government of the Republika Srpska, that there was a broad fuel shortage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know any significant source of fuel for this, the movement of the people from the Srebrenica area outward?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir; and, in fact, what happened was that an arrangement was made where, while the UN agreed to provide the fuel at some juncture, it would not be fast enough for the purposes that they wanted these people out of Potocari starting on the 12th. So what the military did is it went to the Vihor transportation company, a state-owned transportation company in Bratunac, requisitioned the fuel from Vihor; and then, when the UN ultimately provided the fuel, they used that fuel to pay back the state-owned industry for what they had provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a -- there's a series of documents that kind of reflects that trail of where it went, and I believe that there has been testimony, certainly in past trials, to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the -- the next exhibit, 65 ter 2899.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document from the VRS Main Staff under the name of General Petar Skrbic, assistant commander. There's some abbreviations there, but -- for that sector, but who, in your knowledge, was Petar Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the Main Staff's assistant commander for rear services or logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how does this document fit into your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects the legal relationships between the army and the Ministry of Defence at the time, noting the fact that the army can't unilaterally, within its own authority, you know, pull buses from the civilian economy and that this is something that is appropriately or under the competence of the Ministry of Defence. So this is an order, or a request actually, you know, requesting that the Ministry of Defence issue the orders for these buses and place them at the disposal of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And this reference to 50 buses at the Bratunac stadium by 1430, that's the same information we saw in this intercept with Krstic and Krsmanovic. Is that related to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, the time is off by a few hours between 1430 and 1700, but I mean we're talking about, fundamentally, the same situation, that there is an urgent demand for buses to be at these locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter number 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document, again dated 12 July, the Secretariat of the Defence Ministry, Zvornik. The subject is, again: "Request mobilisation of buses." It talks about pursuant to a request by the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska Army; and then, again, talks about 30 buses. Is this consistent with what you've been saying about this process?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Anything else you want to add from this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, I think we've kind of beat this one to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's what I was thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go on to the next document. We're at 65 ter number 59.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're now into a different set of -- a different kind of document from -- something we haven't talked with you about before. But this is from the -- entitled "The Zvornik CJB," or the Public Security Centre, and it comes out under the name of the chief of the CJB, Dragomir Vasic. First of all, before we get into this at all, can you tell us a bit about who Dragomir Vasic was at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995, Dragomir Vasic was the chief of the Zvornik sector for security, public security. As I believe the Court is aware, within the framework of the Republika Srpska, organised on a municipality basis, you had individual sectors for public security; and then, in various regions, you had an overarching command structure known as "the Centre" that these sectors worked for. Dragomir Vasic was the head of the Centre for Public Safety up in Zvornik, and he oversaw a number of municipalities in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And where, to your knowledge of the investigation, was he on July 12, 19 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's not an objection, as such, but Dragomir Vasic is going to give evidence in a week or so time. What's the point in asking this witness all these questions when we can get it from the primary source? We've already had him asked who was Skrbic, who has given evidence. It's really quite a waste of time, this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I completely disagree. There's never a guarantee that a witness will show here. It took about 15, 20 seconds to get out, and I think it's fundamental -- a fundamental reminder about this document and the previous document. I am doing my best not to repeat material that I think the Court is fully aware of; but after such a long period of time, I'm not sure of what I'm fully aware of. But I'm trying to hit the key points and move on. A document -- a first-time document from a key person like this is something that we need more than just a brief discussion of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't agree with you this time, Mr. Haynes. The fact that Mr. Vasic will be here to give evidence shortly doesn't deprive or shouldn't prevent Mr. McCloskey from asking this witness questions about that other witness. So let's proceed. Do you wish Mr. McCloskey to repeat the question, Mr. Butler, or are you in a position to give us an answer? He did start the question: "To your knowledge of the investigation, was he, on July 12th, 1995 ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think he was in Bratunac. I believe the investigation has established that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go over a couple of these points. Number 1: "Acting in accordance with your dispatch, I contacted the civilian commissioner in Bratunac, Miroslav Deronjic." Now, the Court has heard about Miroslav Deronjic and him being the appointed civilian commissioner, so I won't ask you about that, on the invitation of Mr. Haynes. On number 2: "A meeting with General Mladic and General Krstic was held at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters at," the translator's think maybe, "0800 hours, at which tasks were assigned to all those involved." Do you have any information on the meeting at the Bratunac headquarters on the morning of 12 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, my own -- like I say, my own information with respect to, you know, previous trials and the investigation reflects that prior to the third meeting with the UN forces, the VRS -- a number of the VRS commanders and the police commanders who were on the ground did meet, and General Mladic and General Krstic gave various tasks to which units would be located where and what their functions would be for that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's continue, then. Number 3 says: "The military operation is continuing according to plan. The Turks (derogatory term for Muslim) are fleeing towards Suceska, while the civilians have gathered in Potocari ( about 15.000)." How does this conclusion of Mr. Vasic about the Muslims heading towards Suceska fit in with what you've told us about that same subject?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assuming the timing is right - and I think from the Serbo-Croatian version of this behind this, it is in fact 8:00. They are right, the translator - by this time, the senior leadership of the army, General Mladic and of the Drina Corps, General Krstic, are aware that not only of the fact that the military is heading towards Suceska, but that there is an awareness that there is at least 15.000 civilians in Potocari. What they don't appreciate have at this juncture is an appreciation of the size --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Your Honours, I think that none of us is receiving translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What exactly is the problem? Who is not receiving the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It is just that we are on channel 6, and I haven't received it, nor has my expert witness, and I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin, and anybody else? You are also not receiving the translation? All right. It seems that all the accused are not receiving. Okay, so we have a problem. Thank you for informing us. Shall we have another try? Are you receiving interpretation of what I am saying now? All right. So I think the problem is solved. I had nothing to do with it. Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I think you need to repeat the question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you were halfway through your answer, you can probably see on the screen, where you left off.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, if I can continue. While I understand that some of the military forces from the 28th Division are heading towards Suceska it's clear they don't have an appreciation for the sheer number of forces that are going there. It also, again, reflects the fact that they do start to take some preventative measures by sending some police units along the road, given the fact that the army is in a completely different location, most of the army's combat power.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember where Suceska was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Roughly, it is in the -- on the northwest quadrant or side of the Srebrenica enclave. In the area of Suceska and Jaglici village, this is the jumping-off point where the column and the military forces assembled before trying to penetrate the lines and leave the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, number 4, talking about appointing a police chief for Srebrenica, so I won't ask you about that. Number 5, it says: "A meeting will begin at 1000 hours with representatives of UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross and the Muslim representatives of Srebrenica, at which an agreement will be reached on the evacuation of the civilian population from Potocari to Kladanj." Did that happen, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And number 6: "Joint police forces are advancing on Potocari with the aim of taking UNPROFOR personnel prisoner, surrounding the entire civilian population, and cleansing the area of enemy troops." What do you believe -- what forces do you believe Vasic is talking about when he says "joint police forces are advancing on Potocari"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context, he's referring to the joint police forces of the special police of the MUP, which would either be the 2nd Sekovici Detachment or the Jahorina special police, as well as those police companies that were formed off the basis of the municipal MUP organisation. The civilian police who also are designated, when necessary, to form into police companies for military accesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you refer us to any particular document or order that helps you identify which units you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe somewhere, certainly Colonel Borovcanin's after-action report about events that occurred in Srebrenica, lists in detail the specific units that were involved and under his direction at various points in time. I believe there are other references in the documents, not only military but police documents, referring to the Jahorina police as well as the members of the 2nd Sekovici Detachment police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about that 10 July order by Kovac that we've already talked about? I don't remember the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's a laundry list of most of those same units, with the exception of the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was Exhibit 57, for the record. All right. Perhaps we'll wait for the good Mr. Vasic to ask him about the rest of that. Let's go to the next chronological exhibit, 65 ter 156.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's -- we are still on 12 July. It's from the Command of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic. I think we're back to that subject again, Mr. Butler. Could you just briefly deal with it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, General Zivanovic, or the Drina Corps staff, in his name, are forwarding a request to the Main Staff to send fuel. I mean, certainly the Drina Corps does not have, you know, on a disposable level, 10.000 litres of diesel fuel, 2.000 litres of petrol. So they're looking for their headquarters, the Main Staff, to provide that type and quantity of fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Given that you've testified that this fuel is for vehicles to move out the population, what do you make of this comment: "Their final destination is unknown to us for the moment." Can you tell what that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- make sure I read the time right. I mean, this is dated 12 July, 1000 hours. It may very well be, and, in fact, as far as I know, at this point in time the Drina Corps staff does not know what the ultimate destination of these buses is going to be. That decision either has not been yet made by General Mladic or the decision hasn't been translated to the corps staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, we've heard about the destination to Bratunac stadium?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the inbound. It doesn't say the final destinations back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what are you referring to, when you say "destination of those buses," who's in those buses?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those will be the civilians from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what does this indicate to you, if anything, about the planning process as it's occurring at this time on the morning of the 12th?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: From a military perspective, the commands and staffs of all the relevant formations are -- are doing a herculean job, at being able to assemble, on very short notice, the equipment required. There's a lot of work going on and a lot of people are engaged in this process.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you see so far, in looking at these documents and their interrelationships with the other evidence, any hiccups or real problems or significant -- sorry, significant derivations from the JNA/VRS command structure and process that should have been in place on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I mean, given the body of material that we've been talking about, understanding on -- you know, understanding the law and how the VRS worked and the doctrine, I think what you've been looking at, in the context of these orders, are a reflection of how this process should have been working and, in fact, did work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 157.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're still at 12 July 1995, a one-page document. This, again, is it from the Command of the Drina Corps, under the name of General Zivanovic, entitled: "Traffic regulation on the Konjevic Polje-Bratunac road and in the town of Bratunac and orders, commands of the Bratunac Brigade and the Zvornik Brigade, and then it gives both those brigades' orders. Just briefly, can you synopsis what those orders are and how they have to do with any of the -- any of the subjects you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, one of the -- one of the functions of the military police is traffic regulation and control, and this is from the Drina Corps, directing the Zvornik Brigade to establish a traffic control point at this intersection in order to regulate the regulate the transport, the movement of buses through there; as well as to the Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade, that they should coordinate with the local Bratunac police to regulate the traffics going up and down the road to Konjevic Polje from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you say "regulate buses," do you include in that the movement in those buses of the Muslims from Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to the next document, 1107A and C.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're back to an intercept between X and Y at 1200 hours; and as we will soon see, well, it's difficult to make much out of who's talking. We see it talks about buses from various places. Do you know anyone named "Radakovic"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name is not familiar to me, no, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about this comment about "the request for fuel has been forwarded to Krstic"? What does that tell us about -- "Krstic" is a fairly common name. In your view, who do you think this is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context, I believe the correspondents are talking about General Krstic, the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would be -- presumably, from the staff process of trying to do the orders to get additional fuel, any request to the Main Staff or any request to the civilian organisations would have to go out under his name for this type of thing. I'm not aware of any other "Krstic" in the context of the Drina Corps units that would be able to do this at a lower level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, 65 ter 3040.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is another report from the Zvornik CJB. The original is not very clear, but it's from the chief of the CJB, and it's number 278.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just for the record, the 65 ter 59, the previous Vasic document, was numbered -- the CJB number was 277.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So who do you think this document is by?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was drafted by Dragomir Vasic. He was present at the meeting that was -- that this was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it actually says there, as we can see: "Re-dispatch number 277 of 12 July."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll ask you a few things about this. It's now describing this 10.30 meeting that was held at the hotel in Bratunac, "attended by the following." Does that information correspond with information that you have from the investigation, videos, and other information?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We see his conclusions, and there's one in particular I want to ask you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, it's -- it's either -- it looks like it should be on the first page of the B/C/S, but it's number -- in any event, it's number is 3 and 4 on the document, if that can be made out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: 3 says: "They all request free passage for able-bodied men because, allegedly, they are unarmed and they are not in contact with their army in the woods." What do you think that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim -- it sounds like the Muslim leadership at that meeting has informed them that, in fact, there's not one large column, that there are two separate groups: One of them is the army, and the other one is a -- the group of civilians. You know, in this context, it's making it sound like all the civilians who are hiding in the woods are waiting for is a commitment from the VRS that they will be allowed to go as well, and then they'll come in from the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there able-bodied Muslim men among the crowd of Muslims at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And could this reference be a reference to those men?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you take it -- what it says specifically in the above paragraph number 1, where it talks about 10 per cent of the conscripts between 17 and 60, and then look at this one, they also request free passage for the men because they are armed and they are not in contact with their army in the woods. I mean, it could potentially be that same body or it could be a different body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's look at number 4. It says: "It was decided to grant their request and with UNPROFOR assistance (presence and provision of fuel for transportation) and the trucks were provided, boarding of the vehicles will commence at 1400 hours, and escort will be provided until Kladanj." Is that correct, did it happen like that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buses arrived at 1200 hours, from the video evidence that we have; and by 1400, they started moving out, and I believe the evidence shows that they were escorted up to that point, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this is the -- the next comment that he makes is what I'm most interested in. It says: "After the inspection, depending on Mladic's decision, able-bodied men may be allowed to go in order to have the others from the woods to surrender, since our command urged them to do so." What do you make of that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a prior meeting, General Mladic had indicated that he intended that the military-aged men from 17 or 16 to 60 would be screened for their potential involvement in prior war crimes activities. Again, it's indicating the fact that, you know, Mladic may decide at some point in time to allow some of the men to go out and encourage other Muslim males to come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And what I want to ask you, as you are and everyone is well aware, it's the position that the Prosecution that those men in Potocari were designated to be killed sometime in the late hours of 11 July or morning of 12 July. Now, if that is the case - that's the Prosecution's position - what does this comment by Vasic indicate, his knowledge of any potential decision by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's fair to conclude at this juncture that Dragomir Vasic has not been informed of what the ultimate plan is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that reasonable to believe in the circumstances, in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And just on paragraph 5: "Acting upon President Karadzic's order, which was conveyed to us today over the phone, the 2nd Company of the Zvornik PJP shall be dispatched to Srebrenica with a task to secure all facilities of vital importance in the town at all costs and protect them from looting and misappropriation. "It will carry out the task without cooperation of military police which is busy with other tasks. A platoon of this company will lie in ambush at Ravni Buljin, since the Muslim groups were spotted fleeing along this axis." Can you relate this statement with an account of who we refer to him as the Jadar river survivor, who survived an execution along the -- allegedly survived an execution along the Jadar River in the morning of 13 July - we have to go way back to remember that - and his identification of one of the shooters as a guy named Nenad Deronjic? Can you tie up some details for us as it may or may not relate to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I've sat quietly as long as I could, but this is so far away from military analysis as to defy credibility. This is simply an invitation to the witness to put together pieces of the evidence and make what amounts to a second Prosecution speech, and this is precisely the line which I warned we would draw at the start of this man's evidence. This is not borne of any expertise. This is simply evidential analysis by him. It's also the most outrageous leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to be timely, we join.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Likewise, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I agree with Mr. Haynes' point that this is analysis of evidence, but this is precisely what Mr. Butler has been doing for three days, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we've objected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what he's doing is he's, in this case, taking the pieces of the puzzle, whether it be in an intercept or a document, and then he's not making any kind of a judgement on that, and reminding you and us who these people are and how this particular paragraph may relate to the evidence of a survivor. And, you know, very importantly, this -- this is a MUP officer, an important MUP officer. I don't hear an objection from the people that have the most at stake here, and that is the Borovcanin team, because they're very closely related to this MUP officer. They share some of the same units, and these issues can potentially implicate the responsibility of these people, which in my view probably are exculpatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to put some more information with respect to our objection, I'd simply like to recall the Trial Chamber's decision at paragraph 23. This was read already by my colleague, Mr. Haynes, at the beginning of the examination-in-chief of Mr. Butler, but I'd like to recall this further holding by the Trial Chamber which goes as follows: "The testimony of an expert witness with special knowledge in a specific field is intended to enlighten the Judges on specific issues of a technical nature." I don't see the technical nature, and I don't see how this can be helpful to the Judges of this Trial Chamber. The Prosecution likes to say that this Trial Chamber and all Trial Chambers are composed of professional judges. The kind of links that is being offered to the Trial Chamber is simply taking over the role of the Trial Chamber, which is to assess the evidence on the record. Furthermore, Mr. President, for the past about half an hour, and for the past three days, Mr. Butler is making some links and is referring to "the evidence reveals that," or, "my information reveals that." The result of this, Mr. President, will be that we will have to cross-examine Mr. Butler on every single one of these documents and every single one of his answers, and we will be here for ever, unless the modus operandi of this examination-in-chief changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic first, and then you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's going to be very brief. The only reason why we didn't object to this line of question was because Mr. Haynes was faster and then all of a sudden all the counsels raised. So we basically did want to raise this objection, first of all, because the way the question was posed by Mr. McCloskey was a highly leading one, a highly leading one. I believe that Mr. McCloskey was literally giving evidence into the record. Then the other issue is that what Mr. McCloskey indicated and the name that he mentioned, and that this person was a member of the 2nd unit of the PJP is not in the indictment related to Mr. Borovcanin, so this is something that also should be in mind when deciding about our objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I join obviously in the objections by Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Lazarevic, but I think, with all due respect to my friend, the Prosecution, he tells the Court on page 66, line 28, that he's not asking him to give a judgement or to make a judgement; but if you look on just a prior page, on page 65, lines 10 through 11, he does that very thing with Dragomir Vasic, and he's done it throughout. We've been patient, in light of the Court's prior rulings to allow at least some latitude, but he asking him specifically at page 65, lines 11, what his -- for him to conclude at this juncture whether or not he had been informed. If that's not a judgement call, then the Court should perhaps enlighten us. He has been -- it's improper for him to be asked such questions. It is far beyond the purview of this military expert, Mr. Butler, to give that type of evidentiary analysis on the evidence the Court has heard and will hear, especially in light of the fact that you haven't heard the evidence of the Defence yet, and we think we're asking the Court - or we know we are - that you restrict the Prosecution and this witness to confine his testimony to the order that the Court issued. And I would just, for the record, give a standing objection on that for the remainder of his testimony. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey -- Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I would just like to join to the submissions of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the problem here is probably my question. Perhaps people don't remember, but I think the vast majority of my question is based on facts already put forth in this Trial Chamber. If I'd broken it down and gone one by one by one by one, I probably wouldn't have gotten an objection, but these are facts that have been established. This witness knows what unit Nenad Deronjic belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then ask him that question and leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm just trying to save a little time, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we reiterate what we said earlier on the beginning of this, Mr. Butler's testimony, that his testimony ought to be limited to his military expertise. We don't consider the question, as put to you and as it appears between page 65 and 66, falls within those parameters. However, you are free to ask the witness if all examination of Zvornik PJP records, 2nd Company, he can give us any information about Nenad Deronjic, such as being or not being a member thereof. But otherwise, please restrict your questions to military expertise aspects.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, have you -- do you have any information as to what unit Nenad Deronjic belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. He is -- he is a member of the 2nd PJP Company out of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And has his name been mentioned by any survivor?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, is the 2nd PJP Company mentioned in any of the documents relating to the forces that Mr. Borovcanin are under the command of?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Same objection, Mr. President. The form of the question is asked -- my colleague is asking the witness to confirm what is or is not in the evidence. This is not what this witness is here for. This witness is here to say if there is a particular fact that my colleague wants to put to him and say, "Is this in accordance with the doctrine of the VRS forces," that's what he's here to say. He's not here to say whether there is or there is not something in the evidence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the value to this witness is that he is aware of the pieces of the military puzzle and the -- as he's described in depth, and the facts on the ground, and can link them together because of his over-reaching knowledge of this subject. This all goes to his expertise because of his vast knowledge of these military subjects as they relate to these crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The organisation and general procedures of the Republika Srpska Army is an issue which is relevant to this case. The Trial Chamber finds that Butler's experience rendering his opinion on this matter of potential value in assisting the Trial Chamber to understand or determine issues in the dispute. That question and this topic does not fall within that, no way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You ought to read also the preceding paragraph before the ones that you read. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All I can say, Mr. President, is for the last three days, two days, Mr. Butler has been putting the pieces of the puzzle together, based on his knowledge. I don't believe for a minute that you've limited him to -- purely to doctrine. If he can't tell us who he thinks the 2nd PJP unit is under the command of, what can he say? There's no point in going forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we disagree with you, Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Haynes, this time. We consider this question to fall perfectly well within the parameters established by our decision, especially in light of what was asked earlier on, particularly yesterday, in relation to the incorporation of MP units and the involvement of Mr. Borovcanin or the appointment of Mr. Borovcanin. So go ahead and answer the question, which is: "Mr. Butler, now is the 2nd PJP Company mentioned in any of the documents relating to the forces that Mr. Borovcanin are under the command of?" I read it literally as it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In fact, it was when we talked about it, I don't know the 65 ter number, but it's the Republika Srpska MUP order number 64/95, dated 10 July 1995, paragraph 2 specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We're going to need to go back to that order. It's number --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise. It's the 1st Company the PJP that's under that. So, in this context, the special police detachment from Sekovici is not the same as the 2nd Police Company from Zvornik SJB. So in that context, I misspoke. The 2nd Company is not designated as being directly under the command of Colonel Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we could take a break, Your Honour. I mean, for me to have to go through that to get a piece of exculpatory information for Borovcanin is beyond me, since Mr. Butler has been testifying about these precise things over and over again. This is what his narrative does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Calm down. Let's have a 25-minute break. There is no point in getting keyed up on anything. Take the example from us. So we'll have a 25-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Getting away from paragraph 5 in this document to paragraph 6, it says: "The 1st Company is successfully carrying out given tasks." What, in your view -- what unit is this, in your view, the 1st Company?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you -- I'm sorry, could you refer back to which document we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. We're at 65 ter 3040. We're at that Vasic 12 July document. It's the paragraph right after that talk of the 2nd Company, and it just says: "The 1st Company is successfully carrying out given tasks." What -- can you identify what unit you think that is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this context where he would refer to it as the 1st Company, this is the 1st PJP Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you provide any -- we have, I think as you've just testified, the 1st Company was mentioned in the Kovac order with Mr. Borovcanin, and now we have Mr. Vasic reporting on the 1st Company, himself. Can you make any -- give any opinion regarding the command relationships regarding Borovcanin and Mr. Vasic, regarding the 1st Company?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've not come across any information which would suggest that at a -- at this particular juncture, 12 July 1995, that the 1st PJP Company has been resubordinated from the direction of Mr. Borovcanin and, in fact, given back to Mr. Vasic. So the activities, while -- while Mr. Vasic is talking about what they're doing and what -- in a broad sense, this company is still under the control of Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document. It's an intercept, English 1111A, B/C/S is the B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a 12 July intercept at 1220 hours, and it's a conversation between two unidentified men, X and Y. As we see, X says: "What are we going to do about fuel?" Y says: "I don't know. I told Miletic." Then there's some talk about trucks and leaving towns, and then some fuel. Can you, from your analysis, offer an opinion on who you believe Miletic is in this reference?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe, in this context, that the individual that they're referring to -- the correspondents are referring to General-Major Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even though it may be under the direct purview of the assistant commander of logistics of the Main Staff to go through the actual process of obtaining the fuel, certainly this is an issue that General Miletic, as the chief of operations and as the Chief of Staff at the time, you know, would be -- would have to be aware of and, to some degree, engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But why?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular juncture, the orders -- any orders going out to the Ministry of Defence would have to, you know, have his signature on them, as opposed to one of the other staff officials. Well, not necessarily his signature would have to go out under his broader authority; but moreover is the fact that General Miletic would be in the position to know what other potential fuel holdings that other military units of the Army of the Republika Srpska might have and be in a position to authorise the transfer of fuel from one location to another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I let the witness finish. I accept his explanation, in general, but he's speaking about this document, and I would like the Prosecution to present the whole document as it appears, and then he starts his analysis -- and then he can start his analysis on this document, because the problem is the Prosecution read only part of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madame Fauveau. You can't do that yourself on cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President, but the problem is that this is going to lengthen the cross-examination, and perhaps this is not necessary. We could shorten things and work in a more efficient way, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm doing my very best to make reference to things that I think are specific and that affect various subjects; and if there's something in this -- I will continue to try to do that, but I don't want to, nor do I think the Court wants me to read out everything that I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm very sorry, but we heard, for five minutes, about the fact that General Miletic knew something, and this conversation, this intercept says, precisely where the Prosecutor stopped reading: [In English] "He doesn't know, either."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The fact that General Miletic either knows where to get the fuel or doesn't know where to get the fuel shows that he's involved with fuel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but we are starting -- we're starting an argument now. Please proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's try the next exhibit, 1112A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an intercept that is of one page, that we see the entire intercept on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "C" is the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It is at 1240 hours on the 12th, and it's between Panorama, as X, and Y, who is barely audible. Can you remind you, Mr. Butler, if you know who what Panorama or what Panorama is.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The broad phrase "Panorama" refers to -- it's a communications, I won't say, "code word," but it's a word that is used to refer to the Main Staff. We see it often in radio -- in the radio intercepts. It's their code name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: They may need to go to page 2 in the B/C/S to get -- to get the B/C/S up there. Thank you. Thank you, Ms. Stewart. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So we have this person, Y: "We are starting the evacuation of those who want to go towards Kladanj." Then Panorama says: "Okay." Y says: "Pass it on. Just let provide transportation." Then we don't hear from X. Then Y says: "And reinforce with trucks and buses, and a water truck should be sent to give them water and food. This morning we organised it here. We'll give them everything. I talked with them, and we'll accept all the civilians who want to and they can stay. Those who don't want to can choose where they'll go." What, in your view, is Y referring to when he's talking to Panorama?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's talking to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor has just said that Panorama said, on line 9 of the transcript: [In English] "We don't need transportation." [Interpretation] I don't believe this is Panorama.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll just -- I'll talk out that part of the question at this point, just to: What do you think this statement from whoever to whomever means? Then he can tell us if he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madame Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm very sorry, but we can't work like that here. Here, we've got people that are accused of something, and you can't put -- charge them with something and say maybe this concerns them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please answer the question, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way Mr. McCloskey has rephrased it, it becomes new to whoever Y is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. In this context, it doesn't make clear who Y is; but simply at this juncture, the correspondent Y is relating to X, which is listed at Panorama, some organ of the Main Staff, that the evacuation is commencing at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so you think this is a reference to the evacuation of what?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context of time on this particular day, it would be the evacuation of the individuals from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And from what you read in the -- what can you -- what is your evaluation regarding what the plan is for the options, if any, of these -- of these refugees?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are -- you know, this correspondent believes the options are as laid out by General Mladic, that, you know, those who want to stay can stay and those who want to -- don't want to, you know, can choose where they'll go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you refer to General Mladic, is there -- do you have something you can cite to where -- for that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the context of, one, you know, the most immediate document goes back to the report of Dragomir Vasic; and beyond that, looking at the transcripts of the videotaped meetings between the Muslims and the Dutch-Bat and the VRS, which General Mladic presided over on 11 and 12 July, that this is the input from that final meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next intercept. It's 1113A and B. They should be both on page 1, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is at 1250 hours, and at about ten minutes after the one we just heard. And according to this, the conversation is between General Mladic, M, and an unidentified male, X. X says: "Go ahead, General." Mladic says: "Have these buses and trucks left?" X says: "They have." Mladic says: "When?" X says: "About 10 minutes ago." Mladic says: "Good, excellent. Continue to monitor the situation. Don't let small groups of them sneak in. They've all capitulated and surrendered and we'll evacuate them all: Those who want to and those who don't want to." X says: "I understand, General." Mladic says: "Don't issue any statements and don't interrupt them over the" something. "We'll open a corridor towards Kladanj." Then Mladic goes on to say says: "Indeed, let it pas there. Take a patrol of ours to wait on the road, and remove the mines and obstacles... leave the territory." Now, in this, where Mladic is attributed as saying,"They've all capitulated and surrendered," and "We'll evacuate them all," who do you believe in the context of what's going on and in the context of this intercept, Mladic is referring to when he says, "We'll evacuate them all: Those who want to and those who don't want to?"

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he's referring to all those Bosnian Muslims who are at Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And how about this "will open a corridor towards Kladanj," did anything like that happen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I'm not sure whether they're exhibits or not, but there will be a series of orders that follow this from the Drina Corps to the Vlasenica Infantry Brigade, which garrison in that area, which will provide instructions to them as to procedures to take for them to clear some of the barriers away from that road; and then that's going to be the designated terminus point for this convoys, at which point the Bosnian Muslims will proceed to Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This reference to remove the mines and obstacles, what does that have to do with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- they weren't buried mines or obstacles, so to speak. What they were referring to is barriers that had been placed on the road. The road runs through a tunnel. At one side, it's Muslim territory; the other side, it's Serb territory. They're referring to the fact of removing the barriers off the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to another document, 65 ter number 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a different sort of document than we've seen before, entitled: "Republika Srpska MUP, RDB, to the deputy Ministry of the Interior, personally, held of the Public Security Department, MUP of the Republika Srpska, Bijeljina, personally, chief of the RDB Centre, Bijeljina, personally." What is the RDB?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The RDB is the Republika Srpska state security apparatus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us a brief description of the Ministry of Interior police and security, how they're related to each other, just briefly, especially at like the CJB level?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the Ministry of Interior, as it was structured, you had the three component responsibilities. You had public safety, which was administered by the SJBs and the CJBs, those public safety officers and public security offices. You had another wing which was the organisation of the special police units which were nominally designated for use in anti-terrorist types of operations. The reality was, because of the shortage of combat troops, they were often used on the front lines. And the third component relevant to this is the state security apparatus, which is responsible for the maintenance of internal security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How would the state security person in Zvornik be related, if at all, to Dragomir Vasic, for example, the head of the CJB?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He does not work for Dragomir Vasic. The state security apparatus is a separate chain. He's not under the command of the special police, he's not under the command of the local municipal authorities. His line of control runs directly up state security channels to the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe what it is they do, especially in the context of the kind of things we're looking at here; in their documents, I mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I testified I believe Monday or Tuesday, they provided, on behalf of the president, a separate line of information with respect to what was happening in Bosnia to ensure that the information that they were receiving from the army or from other political sources was, in fact, accurate. The RDB was one of those mechanisms doing internal security and reporting on the internal security situation, that the supreme commander, Karadzic, and the Ministry of the Interior used to keep aware of what was going on in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's outside of their normal counter-intelligence-related functions with respect to political and other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell, from this document, whether or not there's a state security person on the ground reporting this, or is he getting it from somewhere -- I mean, can you -- what can you tell us about this -- how this information gets put on this piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the document, apparently they do have somebody on the ground, and I don't know whether it's specifically Mr. Kijac or not, who is gaining with respect to the understanding of what the international humanitarian organisations are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think -- I think we can all read that. I don't think I need to ask you about that at this, unless someone else does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next exhibit, 1114A and in -- in the English, and B.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is an intercept from the 12th of July, 1305 hours, between Krstic and Sobot. At some point, it looks like K says: "Put me back to the switchboard. Miss, put me through to the Vlasenica Brigade." Then as we go down, Krstic says: "Get in touch with these guys from the MUP. That means you, your brigade, and them." The person responds: "I gave everything there is." Krstic says: "Wait, slow down, man. Secure the road first from the crossroad below from where you are 12 kilometres towards" something, "and up to the tunnel." The person says: "To the tunnel? Of course, okay, that's where they'll be disembarking." "Take care nothing must happen to any of them. Okay, is that clear?" "Yes, sir." "Until further notice, secure that part of the road. That's it." "Okay. That's it, chief. Bye." Now, from the various references that we see here, can you make anything out of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person referred to as "Krstic" is General Krstic, and what he's trying to do first is contact an individual named "Kosoric." In this context, there's two Kosorics. One is his own chief of intelligence and the other one is an individual named Mile Kosoric, who is the commander of the Light Infantry Brigade. So I believe he's referring to that particular Kosoric, not his chief of intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what else, as they get to the substance of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I noted before, it talks about, in context with an exhibit two or three ago, the procedure that's being put in place to secure the proposed road, the evacuation route that the buses were going to take to the Kladanj area. That fell into the area of responsibility of the Vlasenica Brigade, and he's tasking the Vlasenica Brigade to do this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And to take care that nothing must happen to any of them, who is he referring to in that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would be talking, in this context, to the Bosnian Muslim individuals being taken from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go on to the next one, 65 ter 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We have another Zvornik CJB document, 12 July. This one is their number 281, with Vasic's name. This gives, as we can see, an update. We see here that Vasic says at one point that: "Sekovici special detachment and the 1st Company of the PJP of the Zvornik CJB and the 5th Company of Zvornik CJB are blocking this section with the goal of destroying these forces." Can you tell us what he's talking about here, when he says "this section"? What section is he talking about, if you can tell from this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The section that he's referring to in this context is the section of the column that we generally understand to be transiting that area at the time. They're blocking, within the contents of the section, those particular areas of the enclave that those MUP forces are garrisoning. They've been set up along that road, along that northern perimeter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to your tab 41, 65 ter 147.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see a document from the Command of the Drina Corps to the VRS Main Staff, Intelligence Affairs Sector, Intelligence Administration, and the Drina Corps Bratunac IKM, personally Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric. It talks about an enemy soldier that was captured, and Drina Corps Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric who is the duty officer. Some other information by Major Pavle Golic. First of all, Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, who is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric is the chief of intelligence of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Major Pavle Golic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Pavle Golic is an intelligence officer who works for Colonel Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what significance, if any, has this document had for your analysis and/or narrative report?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reflects the fact that by the early afternoon of 12 July of 1995, that the intelligence organs of the Drina Corps are starting to receive information from captured Muslims. Those Muslims are being talked to, they're being interrogated to find out what information of value they have. As this report indicates, they are getting intelligence information and are further passing it on to other -- you know, other agencies, in this case to the -- personally toward the forward command post, to make sure that the intelligence officer of the Drina Corps gets this information. One of the larger reoccurring themes that we as part of these reports and which causes problems later down the line for the Zvornik Brigade was that there was always an under-appreciation by the military operations people and the military intelligence people on just how large the column was and how many armed members were part of the column. So this is part of that process, where they're trying to figure out the scope and the combat power of that column from early prisoner of war reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 239.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's a daily combat report from the Bratunac Brigade on St. Peter's Day, which is the 12th of July. Now, what does this report indicate the -- at least the Bratunac Brigade's knowledge of the column and the direction its taking?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As indicated in paragraph 1, you know, at this time in the afternoon, most of the VRS is aware that, in fact, the 28th Infantry Division is not in the Bandera Triangle where they thought it was that previous evening. In fact, it is trying to make a breakout of northern portion of the enclave. So paragraph 1 is just a general awareness of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 7, is that -- that statement regarding the transport of the Muslim population correct, as far as you knew from other documents or evidence on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, at this particular point in time, the movement of the Muslims from Potocari is -- is well underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's go to another document, 65 ter 322.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This time we have a Zvornik Brigade document, a regular combat report of the same date, 12 July, and I just want to ask you about a part that's in the middle of it. It says: "We sent to Bratunac, pursuant to your order, eight buses from Drina-trans, two buses from our VP, and four of our trucks. One military police detachment was sent to Konjevic Polje pursuant to your order." I just want to ask you about what do you think this eight buses from Drina-trans and two buses is about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're part of those initial directions that came on the late night of the 11th or early on 12 July 1995 for the military units to send equipment. I don't believe they specifically reference it, but the Drina Corps order to that effect. They're noticing "your order," although of course they don't give the order number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about this next line: "One military police detachment was sent to Konjevic Polje pursuant to your order"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, there's a Drina Corps order out that specified that the Zvornik Brigade was to establish a military police check-point at that intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that the one you've talked about earlier today?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now let's go to the next one, 65 ter 2748, which we've jumped now to the -- another one of these Main Staff reports to the president of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's dated 12 July, and this is also under the name of General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It hasn't quite come up yet. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd just like you to go, again, to the Drina Corps section, where we see, on page -- it's B/C/S page 3, and English page 3. It's under paragraph 6, and we see a specific update on the Zepa situation. Then we also see that it goes on to say: "The enemy has been attempting to withdraw from the Srebrenica enclave with women and children in the direction of Ravni Buljim and Konjevic Polje, but ran into a minefield." Now, it goes on to talk about the units engaged in carrying Krivaja 95 or carrying out all the combat tasks according to plan. In the course of the day, they liberated the village of Potocari, and they are continuing to advance in order to liberate all the places in the Srebrenica enclave. It says on axis: "Parts of our unit and of the MUP units have laid ambushes in order to destroy Muslim extremists who have not surrendered and who are attempting to break out of the enclave in the direction of Tuzla." Any comment on this information, from your knowledge, anything that's not correct or fits into your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this context, you know, it reflects the Main Staff as being informed by the Drina Corps, for the most part, about what is happening. Some of the information is not accurate, in fact. I don't believe there's any evidence that women and children, in any sizeable number, were accompanying the column, so that's inaccurate information that was being reported up. It --
